profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for a draft decision-support package that a Southeast Michigan planning collaborative wants to pilot with county and city partners. The package translates the Detroit EPA multipollutant risk-based case study into a practical review tool: tract-level PM2.5 maps, local baseline health overlays, subgroup profiles for susceptible/vulnerable populations, and an inequality panel using the Atkinson Index. The agenda is to judge whether the current design is ready for a pilot demo, identify gaps in how local-scale data are represented, and decide what revisions are needed before circulation to partner agencies. The expected outcome is conditional approval of the design with a short list of modifications to the maps, captions, and summary panels.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Environmental Epidemiologist and Health Equity Lead
members.expertise: Health impact assessment, small-area baseline disease burden, environmental justice indicators, inequality metrics
members.background: Former analyst at a state health department who now leads health equity methods for a regional public health institute supporting air quality planning.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot package to be credible with local health departments and community-facing reviewers, and is especially worried that a polished regional summary could hide neighborhood-level inequities or misrepresent what the health baselines mean.
hidden_assumptions: When a design refers to the 'baseline risk' layer, it should mean observed tract-level mortality and asthma hospitalization burden used to identify susceptible populations, not a modeled no-policy counterfactual.
A 'Detroit' pilot should foreground the City of Detroit and its neighborhoods, because that is what local public-health reviewers will assume they are being shown.
A design only truly 'reduces inequality' if none of the named susceptible or vulnerable subgroups are left worse off, even if a summary inequality index improves overall.
If local-scale health data are included, reviewers will interpret them as representing existing community conditions rather than a modeling reference state.

members.name: Arun Mehta
members.role: Air Quality Systems Engineer and Decision-Tool Architect
members.expertise: Emissions scenario modeling, policy evaluation dashboards, spatial exposure surfaces, regulatory planning workflows
members.background: Previously worked on contractor teams supporting regional air-quality analyses and now leads technical design for planning tools at a metropolitan policy lab.
members.private_state: He wants the package approved quickly for the pilot and is trying to preserve continuity with the existing Detroit case-study architecture so the engineering team can reuse data pipelines without reopening the design.
hidden_assumptions: In this kind of planning tool, 'baseline' naturally means the no-additional-controls modeled scenario that all policy alternatives are compared against.
The project geography has already been inherited from the original Detroit metropolitan case-study footprint, so 'Detroit' is shorthand for the broader metro/nonattainment area.
If total health benefits increase and the Atkinson Index improves for the covered area, the design has adequately shown that inequality is reduced.
Neighborhood-specific subgroup concerns belong in interpretation notes, while the core approval standard for a review tool is whether the regional comparison panels are coherent and reproducible.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the baseline risk layer
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about the 'baseline risk map' and 'baseline slides' as if they mean the same starting point.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'baseline' means the observed tract-level pre-policy health burden and exposure pattern used to identify susceptible/vulnerable populations in existing Detroit neighborhoods.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'baseline' means the modeled no-new-controls reference scenario against which the policy alternatives are compared in the tool.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In policy evaluation work, 'baseline' is such a routine term that both hear it as standard jargon; the slides can look sensible under either interpretation, so nothing in a normal design review forces the distinction into the open.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the Detroit rollout
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the upcoming 'Detroit rollout' or 'Detroit pilot' as though the target geography is obvious.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the pilot should center on the City of Detroit and its neighborhoods, with metro views as secondary context.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the pilot covers the Detroit metropolitan/nonattainment area inherited from the original case-study setup, with city views as a drill-down option.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Project materials and everyday speech commonly switch between 'Detroit' and 'Detroit metro,' and because both geographies are legitimate in this context, each person hears the same phrase as confirming their own boundary for the review.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the equity check to pass
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the design should show 'reduced inequality' or that the 'equity check passes.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the equity check passes only if each named susceptible/vulnerable subgroup avoids worsening, not merely if the aggregate inequality metric moves in the right direction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the equity check passes if the Atkinson Index and total health-benefit summaries improve for the covered geography, even if some subgroups do not improve individually.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both already endorse the same moral goal and both accept using the Atkinson Index, the surface agreement feels complete; the hidden difference is in the standard of sufficiency, which design reviewers rarely restate explicitly.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to survive contact with local health departments and community-facing reviewers. If the package looks polished but blurs tract-level mortality and asthma burden, they'll lose trust immediately. I also want the inequality story to be legible at the neighborhood scale, not just in a regional summary.
turns.utterance: Before we call this ready, I want to make sure the pilot package will actually hold up in partner review. The local-scale health overlays, the subgroup profiles, and the inequality story all need to land clearly for people who are going to read this from a public-health perspective.

turns.inner_thought: The current architecture is already enough for a pilot if we don't reopen scope. We've got the modeled no-additional-controls baseline wired into the strategy comparison, and the Atkinson panel plus total benefits should satisfy the equity check for the metro case-study footprint. I just need approval to keep continuity with the existing build.
turns.utterance: From the design side, we're pretty close. The current package has the baseline risk map, the side-by-side strategy cards, and a reduced-inequality summary panel, and together those should give partners a coherent pilot review set.

turns.inner_thought: What I need to know is whether the baseline risk map is showing the existing tract-level disease burden people in Detroit neighborhoods already recognize, and whether the Detroit rollout starts with the city and its neighborhoods rather than a wider regional frame. If it opens too broad, reviewers will think we're dodging the hardest questions.
turns.utterance: Can I just check two things on that? First, will the baseline risk map reflect the burden patterns local reviewers are going to recognize right away, and second, does the Detroit rollout open with city-facing views rather than making people dig for them?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, because the baseline layer is already inherited from the existing Detroit metro/nonattainment architecture. Once the reference run is loaded, the main maps and cards will populate without much extra work. City views can sit as drill-downs under the metro shell; that still counts as Detroit-first to me.
turns.utterance: Yes, that should be straightforward. The baseline layer is already wired from the Detroit case-study geography, and once the reference run is loaded for the rollout, the opening sequence should come together without much rework.

turns.inner_thought: I need the tool to visibly show if Southwest Detroit or any other high-susceptibility tract is left behind. An overall index improvement is not enough if one of the named vulnerable groups gets worse. Reviewers will ask that immediately, especially if we're calling this a Detroit pilot.
turns.utterance: Okay. Then for me the key thing is that the equity check visibly flags if places like Southwest Detroit, or other high-susceptibility tracts, do not improve even when the top-line summary looks positive. If we're saying reduced inequality, people need to be able to see that it really passes.

turns.inner_thought: I can agree with the spirit of that without changing the approval standard. For the pilot, if overall benefits go up and the Atkinson Index improves across the Detroit metro area, the equity check passes. We can always add notes or callouts for specific tracts, but I don't want subgroup-by-subgroup pass criteria to hold up the build.
turns.utterance: I agree that we should make that visible. At the same time, if the Atkinson trend improves for Detroit overall, that gives us a solid basis for saying the equity check passes in the pilot review, and then we can support that with the tract callouts.

turns.inner_thought: I need the captions to make clear that the baseline maps are about existing mortality and asthma burden in local neighborhoods. Otherwise health partners may read them as something more abstract and miss the point of why those tracts matter. The wording has to anchor the maps in current community conditions.
turns.utterance: One revision I'd strongly suggest is tightening the baseline captions so they clearly anchor the maps in mortality and asthma burden. That way health partners will read them as the local starting point rather than just another technical layer.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable as long as I don't have to change the underlying metro structure. I can keep the appendix and some comparison panels at metropolitan scale, preserve the existing pipeline, and make the front of the deck feel city-centered enough that everyone hears 'Detroit rollout' the way they've been using it.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can keep the appendix at metro scale while making the main deck feel Detroit-first, which is consistent with the current rollout plan and should help the partner audience orient quickly.

turns.inner_thought: I'm close to yes, but only if the summary doesn't overclaim. Nontechnical reviewers need to trust that 'reduced inequality' means no named vulnerable subgroup is being sacrificed behind a cleaner-looking index. If the message is explicit and readable, I can support moving it forward.
turns.utterance: With those adjustments, I'm comfortable calling the design nearly ready. I just want the reduced-inequality message to stay explicit and easy for nontechnical reviewers to trust when they move from the maps to the summary panel.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that's enough to proceed. I'll finalize the pilot build using the existing reference scenario and regional comparison panels, tune the captions so they read more clearly to health partners, and tighten the equity slide language around the Atkinson result. That should get partner review out the door quickly without reopening the architecture.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll finalize the pilot build and make the revisions to the baseline and equity slides before we send the package out for partner review.
